 19. The principle that legal burden of proof always remains on the prosecution is the most fundamental principle of our Criminal Jurisprudence and is much older than The Evidence Act because it was the common law administered by Apex Courts of Sub-Continent. Elementary criminal law, thus, is that in all cases burden of proof lies upon prosecution to bring the guilt home to the door of the accused beyond doubt. If at the end of and on the whole of the case there is a reasonable doubt engendered by the evidence given either by prosecution or the accused the accused is entitled to an acquittal. It is, also. to be borne in mind that doubt must be real, genuine and well founded which a normal man with normal intelligence in a given circumstances would normally harbor. It is to be kept in view that golden thread of proof beyond reasonable doubt should not be morbidly stretched to embrace any degree of doubt at the expense of social defence. 

 44. Abscondence of convict-appellant now is dealt with True it is that the convict-appellant was non abscondence and he was tried in absentia but it is equally true that abscondence of an accused does not automatically amount to evidence of guilty mind and abscondence is equally consistent with innocence and guilt. Abscondence cannot always be a circumstance to lead to inference of guilt of the accused and sometimes out of fear and self respect and to avoid unnecessary harassment a person indicted as an accused may remain in abscondence of course abscondence of the accused in the fact and circumstances of a case, sometimes may furnish corroboration of the prosecution evidence.
